name: Gold-silver ratio reversion

origin.source_title: Investigating the relationship between gold and silver prices (Journal of Forecasting 17(2), 81-107)

how_it_works.simple: Count how many ounces of silver buy one ounce of gold. When it takes far more than usual, swap gold for silver; when it takes far fewer, swap back.
how_it_works.analogy: Like two siblings who usually walk together: when one runs far ahead, bet that the gap closes.
how_it_works.precise: If log gold and log silver prices are cointegrated, deviations of the ratio from its long-run level should shrink. Escribano and Granger test this on 1971 to 1990 monthly data with error correction models; cointegration holds only in some periods and needs shifts in the long-run level, and the forecasting gain does not survive out of sample for silver.

rule: Our simple version, for testing: each month, compute log(gold / silver) and its z-score against the past 5 years; above +2 hold silver and short gold, below -2 the reverse, close at the mean. This rule is ours.
data_needed: World Bank Pink Sheet monthly gold, silver and platinum prices (free, DAT-0035)
economic_rationale: Both are precious metals priced by many of the same investors, and some industrial and jewellery demand can switch between them, so their prices should not drift apart forever.
why_it_might_fail: The source paper finds the relation unstable: cointegration needs breaks in the long-run level, and out of sample the silver forecasts lose to a random walk. The ratio's long-run level has shifted, so 'normal' may not exist. Silver is far more industrial than gold.

reported_results.source: Escribano and Granger (1998), Journal of Forecasting, abstract (author repository)
reported_results.notes: Abstract: cointegration could have occurred during some periods, especially during and after the 1979 to 1980 bubble, but intercept dummies are needed over the full sample. Non-linear error correction models beat the random walk for gold in and out of sample; for silver they beat it in sample but lose that out of sample. A forecasting study with no trading returns or costs.

post_publication_evidence: Not checked by us yet. We found no peer-reviewed out-of-sample trading test of the ratio net of costs.

relevance.reason: The gold-silver ratio is one of the most popular retail metals trades and is often sold as a sure thing; free monthly data covers both metals.

research.notes: Testable on World Bank monthly gold and silver; short selling a metal needs futures, so a test would use the ratio as a proxy. Added in Amanda's metals batch on 2026-10-25.
